title: How to Analyze Customer Feedback in a Multi-Sided Marketplace
summary: Analyze multi-sided marketplace feedback with one shared taxonomy, split by audience, then measure each theme's impact against each side's own score.
body_markdown:
A marketplace has more than one customer. A delivery platform serves the people who order, the drivers who deliver, and the merchants who prepare the order. A grocery marketplace adds personal shoppers and advertisers. Each side leaves feedback in its own channel, in its own words, about its own version of the same event. A late delivery is a cold meal to the consumer, a wasted wait to the driver, and a refund request to the merchant.


To analyze customer feedback in a multi-sided marketplace, run every side's feedback through one shared theme taxonomy. Tag each comment with the side it came from. Then measure each theme's impact against each side's own score. Thematic supports this by applying one bottom-up theme set across surveys, support tickets, and app reviews. Metadata filters then split any theme by audience without a separate analysis per side.


Below are the six steps, examples from two marketplaces, and the mistakes that make cross-side analysis give the wrong answer.


## The six-step process for multi-sided feedback analysis


1. **Map every side and every channel it uses.** List each audience and where its feedback lands.
2. **Build one taxonomy with a shared trunk.** Keep common themes identical across sides and add side-specific branches underneath.
3. **Tag every comment with its side.** Carry audience, region, and order or event data into the analysis.
4. **Trace one event across sides.** Follow a single operational failure through each audience's complaints.
5. **Measure impact per side.** Score each theme against the metric that side actually reports.
6. **Route the fix to the side that is hurting.** Compare impact across sides before deciding who owns the problem.


## Step 1: Map every side and every channel it uses


Start with an inventory, not a dashboard. For each side, write down who they are, how many there are, and every place their words show up.


Sides rarely share channels. Consumers leave app store reviews and answer post-order surveys. Drivers or shoppers answer worker surveys and contact a dedicated support line. Merchants file support tickets and answer partner surveys. If you read only the consumer[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) , you're analyzing one side of a platform whose value depends on all of them. Economists call this the cross-side network effect: each group's value depends on participation from the[other side of the market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-sided_market) . Harvard Business Review's[strategies for two-sided markets](https://hbr.org/2006/10/strategies-for-two-sided-markets) describes the same link between groups such as consumers and merchants.


The common mistake here is treating a worker or merchant survey as an HR or partnerships concern. It's customer feedback about the same product.


## Step 2: Build one taxonomy with a shared trunk


Every side needs to be read against the same set of themes, or you can't compare them. If consumer feedback has a theme called "late delivery" and driver feedback has one called "long wait at pickup," the connection between them depends on someone noticing.


Structure the taxonomy in two layers:


- **Shared trunk themes** describe the event itself: delivery timing, order accuracy, item availability, app reliability, payments and refunds.
- **Side-specific branches** sit underneath and describe how each audience experiences it: "food arrived cold" for consumers, "wait at pickup" for drivers, "refund disputes" for merchants.


Thematic discovers themes[bottom-up from the text](https://getthematic.com/insights/inductive-thematic-analysis) rather than forcing comments into a predefined list. It then applies one theme set across every source. That keeps the trunk identical whether a comment came from a consumer review or a merchant ticket.


## Step 3: Tag every comment with its side


A shared taxonomy only helps if you can split it again. Every comment needs its audience attached, along with any operational metadata you have: region, store or restaurant, order value, and ideally the order or delivery ID.


The side tag is usually easy because the channels differ. The order ID is harder and more valuable. It lets you join a consumer's complaint, the driver's note, and the merchant's ticket about the same delivery.


Thematic supports unlimited metadata filters on the same theme set. You can view "delivery timing" for consumers only, then for drivers only, without rebuilding anything. When[integrating feedback sources](https://getthematic.com/insights/integrate-feedback-sources-analytics-platform) , data without a native connector can arrive through Snowflake, BigQuery, or the API with its metadata intact.


## Step 4: Trace one event across sides


Pick one operational failure and follow it through every audience. The table below is an illustrative example of how a single late delivery can surface.


**Side** **What they experienced** **How it shows up in feedback** **Channel**


Consumer Food arrived late and cold "Order took an hour, food was cold" App review, post-order survey


Driver Waited at the restaurant for the order "Stood at pickup for 25 minutes, lost my next job" Worker survey, support


Merchant Customer demanded a refund "Refunded an order that wasn't our fault" Partner support ticket


Read in silos, these are three unrelated themes owned by three teams. Read together, they're one event. The root cause might sit with any side. A kitchen running behind makes the driver wait, which makes the consumer angry, which lands a refund on the merchant.


A large online grocery marketplace ran into the same pattern with a different event. It serves roughly 10 million consumers, 500,000 personal shoppers, and 40,000 retailers, plus advertisers. The team had been reading feedback in silos, one app at a time.[Analyzing app reviews](https://getthematic.com/insights/sentiment-analysis-of-reviews) from the consumer app and the retailer partner apps together helped the team see how a single out-of-stock product can affect the consumer, the shopper, the retailer, and the advertiser in different ways.


## Step 5: Measure impact per side


Volume tells you which side complains most. It doesn't tell you which side a problem is hurting. Consumers usually outnumber merchants by orders of magnitude, so a volume ranking will hand every priority to the consumer side.


Measure impact against each side's own metric instead. For each theme, compare the average score of people who mention it with the overall average for that side. A theme that barely moves consumer NPS might pull merchant NPS down sharply. That's the signal volume hides.


Thematic's[impact analysis](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) measures that gap. Run it once per side, using the same trunk themes, and you get a side-by-side view of where each theme costs the most. It's the same principle behind why[your most common complaints aren't your biggest problems](https://getthematic.com/insights/most-common-complaints-arent-biggest-problems) , applied across audiences instead of within one.


## Step 6: Route the fix to the side that is hurting


Now compare. For each trunk theme, you have three questions answered:


- **Where does it originate?** Which side's feedback describes the cause rather than the symptom.
- **Where does it hurt most?** Which side's score drops furthest among people who mention it.
- **Where can it be fixed?** Which team owns the product or policy that controls it.


These answers often point at different sides. The complaint may be loudest from consumers, the damage largest among merchants, and the fix in the driver app. Assign ownership by where the fix lives, and measure success by the side that was hurting.


## A worked example: DoorDash


DoorDash runs a three-sided delivery platform: consumers who place orders, merchants who fulfill them, and Dashers who deliver them. DoorDash used Thematic to analyze tens of thousands of NPS responses from customers, drivers, and merchants.


Merchant feedback surfaced a problem the consumer side would never have described. Merchants reported slow menu editing, with repetitive scrolling after every update.


DoorDash redesigned the menu interface. Load times for menu edits fell from 11 seconds to under 3 seconds, and merchant satisfaction increased. Read more about how[DoorDash's research team works](https://getthematic.com/insights/doordash-research-fast-and-flexible) .


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Running a separate taxonomy per side.** You can't compare themes that have different names. Use one shared trunk and add side-specific branches.
- **Ranking themes by combined volume.** The biggest side wins every ranking. Measure impact against each side's own score.
- **Averaging sides into one platform score.** A single blended NPS hides a merchant exodus behind happy consumers. Report each side separately.
- **Dropping operational metadata.** Without order, region, or merchant IDs you can't trace one event across sides. Carry metadata through ingestion.
- **Assigning the problem to the side that complains.** Complaint location and root cause are often different. Route the fix to where it can be made.


## The short answer


Analyzing customer feedback in a multi-sided marketplace means reading every side against one shared taxonomy, splitting it by audience, and measuring impact against each side's own metric. Thematic makes that a filter change rather than three separate projects. It applies one theme set across every source and ranks themes by score impact rather than mention count.


Try this with your current data. Take your top five consumer complaints, find the same five themes in driver and merchant feedback, and check which side each one is actually hurting.
